slides.title: Finding the bytes starts with finding their mapping
keyPoints: Translation and data retrieval are separate work
The MMU checks mappings and permissions
C++ bounds remain a separate contract
slides.narration: A load asks for a value, but the processor must interpret the address under the current address-space context before using the backing location. The memory-management unit, or MMU, supports that translation and protection work. A translation lookaside buffer, or TLB, remembers useful translations so a full table walk is not required every time. These structures do not understand the bounds of a C++ vector. An access can pass page checks and still violate the language’s object rules. Keep the explanation layered: language validity, translation permission, and data availability answer different questions about the same apparent load.

slides.title: Count translation work without pretending to time hardware
keyPoints: One model entry remembers the last page
Repeated page access hits that entry
Data residency is an independent input
slides.narration: The model touches pages four, four, nine, and four. With one translation entry, the first four misses and fills the entry; the second hits; nine misses and replaces four; the last four misses again. The program therefore reports three walks. A separate input says whether data is cached, producing hit, miss, hit, and hit independently of the translation outcomes. These are deliberately selected states, not measurements from a CPU. They show that a TLB hit can accompany a data miss and a TLB miss can accompany a data hit. A real trace would require hardware-specific observation and a careful measurement method.

slides.title: A TLB miss is not automatically a page fault
keyPoints: A valid table walk can fill the missing cache entry
Faults involve an unresolved or forbidden access
The two events need different diagnostic evidence
slides.narration: If the translation cache lacks page twelve but the page table contains a valid permitted mapping, the processor can obtain the mapping and continue. That is a translation miss without a page fault. If the walk instead finds no usable mapping or discovers a forbidden operation, software handling may be required. Mixing the terms makes performance reports misleading: many TLB misses can occur while no disk read or recoverable page fault occurs at all. The chapter’s model explicitly increments walks and returns no mapping only when the table lacks an entry. Interpret those counters according to their definitions rather than treating every slow access as the same event.

question.prompt: Can a page-table walk complete successfully after a TLB miss?
question.answer: Yes. A valid permitted table entry can supply the translation without a page fault.

slides.title: A cached page number needs an address-space identity
keyPoints: The same page number can map different frames
Page-only lookup reuses the wrong context
Include address-space identity in the model key
slides.narration: Both modeled processes request virtual page one, but process A maps it to frame seven and B maps it to frame nine. The intentionally incomplete cache keys only by page, so B receives the earlier seven. The corrected cache keys by the pair of address-space identifier and page, so B receives nine. The output names both results. This program uses maps to expose identity; it does not configure a hardware TLB or measure context-switch behavior. Real hardware and kernels use architecture-specific tagging and invalidation mechanisms. The general invariant is the same: a cached result must belong to the context under which it is reused.

slides.title: Where the simple approach fails
keyPoints: Equating every TLB miss with a page fault overcounts OS work. A page-table walk can succeed normally.
A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Update the page table while continuing to trust an old TLB entry. The next hit returns stale frame information.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Invalidate or update cached translations under the platform’s rules when mappings change. This lab uses clear to make that dependency observable.

slides.title: MMU
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: The memory-management unit, or MMU, is the processor machinery involved in translation and access checking.
It interprets the configured address-space structures according to architectural rules.
Its implementation can include several translation caches and page-walk optimizations.
The MMU does not understand a source-level vector or ownership model.
slides.narration: The memory-management unit, or MMU, is the processor machinery involved in translation and access checking. It interprets the configured address-space structures according to architectural rules. Its implementation can include several translation caches and page-walk optimizations. The MMU does not understand a source-level vector or ownership model. It knows translation and permission information at the architecture’s supported granularity. This explains why a legal machine address can still produce undefined behavior in C or C++: the language may forbid an access that hardware page checks permit.

slides.narration: A translation lookaside buffer, or TLB, caches translations and associated permission information. A matching entry can supply the physical-frame relationship without a complete new walk. Real processors may have distinct instruction and data TLBs, multiple levels, and different handling for page sizes. TLB entries must be interpreted in the correct address-space context. Hardware and kernels can use address-space identifiers and other mechanisms to retain useful entries across switches without confusing one process’s mapping with another’s. Do not assume either that every switch flushes every translation or that retaining entries requires no context tagging.

slides.title: Caching permissions makes invalidation part of correctness
keyPoints: Translation entries can retain access information
Table updates can make cached results stale
Revocation must cover every path using the old entry
slides.narration: Suppose a cached entry allows writing, then the page table is changed to deny it. A lookup that keeps reusing the older permission can violate the intended protection policy even if its frame number is unchanged. Cached translations therefore need invalidation rules, not just eviction rules for capacity. The source lab clears its model TLB explicitly and observes an extra walk on the next lookup. That is a useful model of invalidation’s effect, but it does not implement multicore shootdowns or hardware update ordering. In a real kernel, mapping changes and cache coordination belong to one carefully defined operation.
actions: Require a concrete mapping, access, or state example before revealing the answer.

question.answer: Yes. Its cached permissions or other relevant translation state may be stale.

slides.title: Translation reach counts pages, not useful bytes alone
keyPoints: Nominal reach = entries × page size
Scattered tiny values can touch many pages

slides.narration: A teaching TLB with sixty-four entries and four-kibibyte pages has a nominal reach of two hundred fifty-six kibibytes. Putting those bytes in a compact array could greatly reduce the page working set. The nominal product is only a first estimate: associativity, separate instruction and data structures, and mixed page sizes affect real behavior. slides.title: Retaining entries across switches requires context discipline
keyPoints: Some translations may survive a switch
Tagging prevents unrelated mappings from colliding logically
No universal full-flush claim follows from the word switch
slides.narration: Our incomplete-key demonstration explains why retaining entries without context would be unsafe. It does not prove that every context switch must clear the entire translation cache. Architecture-supported address-space identifiers and kernel policies can retain useful entries while distinguishing contexts. Other operations still require invalidation when mappings change. Therefore, a performance explanation should not assume either universal flushing or unlimited safe retention. Ask which hardware, which switch, and which mapping update is involved. The model teaches the need for identity; the implementation details determine the actual cost. This distinction keeps a portable software lesson from turning into an incorrect claim about every processor.
actions: Require a concrete mapping, access, or state example before revealing the answer.

question.prompt: Why is “every process switch flushes every TLB entry” too strong?
question.answer: Hardware and kernel mechanisms may tag and retain relevant entries while preserving address-space separation.

slides.title: A cache model needs a stated replacement policy
keyPoints: The source map has no capacity limit
Our one-entry model replaces on every different page
Neither model predicts a real processor’s full policy
slides.narration: The source lab stores translations in a map and never evicts them except on explicit clear. That cleanly demonstrates hits, misses, absent mappings, and invalidation. It is not a model of a finite hardware TLB’s replacement behavior. Our added one-entry demonstration supplies a capacity and an obvious replacement rule to make repeated misses visible. When extending either model, state the number of entries and the eviction policy before comparing hit rates. A change in those assumptions can alter the result without any arithmetic error. Avoid presenting a model counter as measured hardware evidence simply because both are called walks.

slides.title: Diagnose the level that actually missed
keyPoints: Translation miss: mapping lookup work
Data-cache miss: byte retrieval work
Page fault: software handles an unresolved access
slides.narration: A slow memory access can involve several events, and one event does not uniquely identify the others. A TLB miss may lead to a successful table walk. The requested data may already be cached. A data-cache miss may occur with a perfectly good cached translation. A page fault may require no disk I/O if the kernel supplies a demand-zero page. When investigating a workload, record which event the measurement source counts and what denominator it uses. Then design a controlled change, such as packing data into fewer pages, to test the translation hypothesis rather than merely hoping any locality change helps.

slides.title: Keep cached answers tied to their full contract
keyPoints: Cache key includes relevant context
Cached data includes permission meaning
Invalidation preserves agreement with authoritative mappings
slides.narration: Translation hardware illustrates a reusable systems lesson: a cached answer is safe only when its key, contents, and lifetime match the authoritative state. Page number alone can omit address-space identity. Frame number alone can omit permission changes. An entry that never expires can outlive the mapping it describes. The compiler cannot discover these semantic omissions in a map key or struct. Tests should switch contexts with equal page numbers, look up an absent mapping, repeat a successful lookup, and invalidate before looking again. Those cases give evidence about the model’s promises while leaving real hardware timing to a separate measurement task.
